title: The von Neumann concept (Von-Neumann-Konzept) and program execution
summary: This unit explains the von Neumann concept, including its four functional units (Vier Werke), a shared main memory (Hauptspeicher) for programs and data, and sequential instruction execution (sequenzielle Befehlsausführung). It also covers the Harvard architecture (Harvard-Architektur), linking (Linken), self-modifying code (selbstmodifizierender Code), and the roles of the prologue (Prolog) and epilogue (Epilog).
concepts: Programs and data in the same memory (Programme und Daten im selben Speicher)
keyFacts: The stack is located in byte-addressable main memory.
The prologue sets up the stack frame, and the epilogue tears it down.
The calling convention specifies which registers must be preserved.
With -O2, register allocation or instruction order may differ from unoptimized examples.
The von Neumann concept separates the computer's structure from the specific problem; the program controls the general-purpose computer.
The four functional units are main memory, the control unit, the arithmetic unit (ALU), and the input/output unit.
In the von Neumann model, programs and data reside in the same main memory.
Main memory consists of equally sized cells with consecutive addresses.
Programs and data are represented as encoded memory contents, or binary codes.
Instructions are generally stored and executed sequentially at ascending addresses.
Conditional and unconditional jumps can change the sequential order.
Von Neumann uses a shared program and data memory, while Harvard uses separate memories.
A shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches is one example of a hybrid organization.
Write protection and the separation of program and data memory are different questions.
Linking combines compiled program modules and libraries, resolves references, and may adjust address values.
Self-modifying code changes its own program code and is a rare exception today.

questions.prompt: Where is the stack located in the computer model under consideration?

options.text: In main memory
Exclusively in the registers
In a stack memory separate from main memory
In the input/output unit

questions.explanation: The stack is an area of byte-addressable main memory. It is not a separate memory apart from main memory.

questions.prompt: At the end of a routine comes the ___, which restores saved values and releases the stack frame.

options.text: Epilogue
Instruction cycle
Linker
Prologue

questions.explanation: The epilogue tears down the frame set up by the prologue and prepares to return.

questions.prompt: Which mappings to the four functional units are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The arithmetic unit is responsible for input and output, including secondary storage.
The control unit carries out the instruction cycle.
The input/output unit translates source code into machine instructions.
The arithmetic unit, or ALU, performs arithmetic operations.
Main memory, or primary storage, contains programs and data.

questions.explanation: Main memory, the control unit, and the arithmetic unit correspond to mappings a, b, and c. Translation is not the task of the input/output unit, while input and output belong to that unit.

questions.prompt:
Which step immediately follows the routine body in the diagram?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
P["Prologue"] --> R["Routine body"]
R --> E["Epilogue"]
E --> C["Return"]
```

options.text: Stack pointer
Return
Prologue
Epilogue

questions.explanation: The epilogue follows the routine body. It restores saved values and releases the stack frame.

questions.prompt: Which fundamental idea is part of the von Neumann concept?

options.text: A computer consists exclusively of an ALU.
The computer's structure is independent of the problem; the program controls the general-purpose computer.
The computer's structure is rebuilt for each problem.
Programs must never be stored in main memory.

questions.explanation: The von Neumann concept describes a general-purpose computer whose specific behavior is determined by the program being run.

questions.prompt: In the von Neumann model, programs and data are stored in the same main memory.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A shared main memory for programs and data is a central feature of the von Neumann model.
concepts: Programs and data in the same memory

questions.prompt: Instructions are generally stored one after another at ___ addresses.

options.text: external only
ascending
descending
random

questions.explanation: The general pattern is storage at ascending addresses. Jumps can later change the execution order.

questions.prompt: Which statements about data and instructions as memory contents are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Instructions are encoded according to the ISA and can be represented as assembly language.
Data are encoded in binary and require an agreed interpretation of their bit patterns.
Instructions, but not data, exist as memory contents.
The readable assembly representation is identical to the physical memory contents.
Data are always stored in memory as decimal digits.

questions.explanation: Both data and instructions are encoded memory contents. They are interpreted differently: data follow an agreed encoding, while instructions follow the ISA.

questions.prompt: What memory organization does the Harvard architecture describe?

options.text: Only memory for instructions, with no data memory
A shared main memory with no registers
Separate program and data memories
A shared memory for programs and data

questions.explanation: Harvard separates program memory from data memory. A shared memory is instead characteristic of von Neumann.

questions.prompt: What is a central task of the linker?

options.text: It changes only the program's input data.
It combines compiled program modules and libraries and resolves references.
It executes the program step by step.
It replaces the ISA with a different ISA.

questions.explanation: The linker combines compiled modules and library components. In doing so, it resolves references and may adjust address values.
concepts: Programs and data in the same memory

questions.prompt: Self-modifying code changes its own program instructions in memory. Today, it is considered a rare exception; different execution paths are usually implemented with conditional jumps and changes to addresses. Statement: Self-modifying code is a common standard technique today.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The statement is false: self-modifying code is considered a rare exception today. Different execution paths are usually implemented with conditional jumps and changes to addresses.

questions.prompt: In the von Neumann model, which task belongs to the control unit?

options.text: Carry out the instruction cycle
Perform arithmetic operations
Provide input and output, including secondary storage
Store programs and data permanently

questions.explanation: The control unit carries out the instruction cycle. Arithmetic operations belong to the arithmetic unit, and storage belongs to main memory.

questions.prompt: A program starts at address $100$. The instruction at $101$ is an unconditional jump to $200$. Which sequence gives the first addresses executed?
questions.explanation: First, $100$ is executed, followed by the jump instruction at $101$. Because the jump unconditionally goes to $200$, $200$ is the next address; $102$ is skipped.

options.text: The control unit controls the arithmetic unit.

questions.prompt: A computer has shared main memory for programs and data, but separate caches for instructions and data. What is this organization called?

options.text: A pure von Neumann computer with no separate memory areas
Self-modifying memory
Strict Harvard architecture
The hybrid organization described

questions.explanation: The hybrid organization described combines shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches.

questions.prompt: Which activities are part of linking? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Execute every instruction during linking
Resolve references between the combined modules
Redefine the target processor's ISA
Adjust address values if necessary
Combine compiled program modules and required library components

questions.explanation: Linking combines modules, resolves their references, and may adjust addresses. Executing the program and defining the ISA are not part of linking.

questions.prompt: During linking, references between the combined program modules are ___, and address values may be adjusted.

options.text: resolved
ignored
encrypted
duplicated

questions.explanation: The linker matches references to their corresponding targets, thereby resolving them. Address values are adjusted if necessary.

questions.prompt: Write protection and the separation of program and data memory are different questions.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: For example, a memory area can be read-only without that automatically determining whether program and data memories are separate.
concepts: Programs and data in the same memory

questions.prompt: What does self-modifying code mean?

options.text: A compiler optimization level of 2
A program that only reads its input data
A linker that combines libraries
A program that changes its own program code

questions.explanation: Self-modifying programs change their own program code. This is different from changing data or from linking.

questions.prompt: A program contains instructions at addresses $40$, $41$, and $42$. The instruction at $41$ is a conditional jump to $100$, and the condition is met. Which address is executed next?
questions.explanation: The jump instruction at $41$ sets the continuation to the target address $100$. Therefore, the normally next address, $42$, does not follow.

questions.prompt: What must remain unchanged in a compiler optimization even if the internal implementation changes?

options.text: The use of -O2
Exactly the same register allocation
Exactly the same instruction sequence
The externally observable behavior required of the program

questions.explanation: Optimizations may change register allocation and instruction order. What matters is that the program's externally observable behavior is preserved.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe program execution? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The basic instruction sequence is initially carried out sequentially.
Every jump must completely prohibit sequential ordering.
An optimization may work differently internally as long as the observable behavior is preserved.
Optimization necessarily means using the same register allocation as in the example.
Conditional and unconditional jumps can change the order.

questions.explanation: Sequential execution is the starting point, jumps can depart from it, and optimizations may change the internal implementation. Register allocation does not have to remain the same.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes memory organization from memory handling?

options.text: Separate memory areas cannot be write-protected.
A shared memory can never have different access permissions.
Whether program and data memory are organized together or separately is a different question from write protection.
Write protection automatically determines whether the architecture is Harvard or von Neumann.

questions.explanation: Whether memory is shared or separate concerns its organization. Write protection, by contrast, describes how memory areas are handled.
concepts: Programs and data in the same memory

questions.prompt: Which statements about von Neumann, Harvard, and the hybrid organization described are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Harvard uses separate program and data memories.
Write protection alone turns every shared memory into a Harvard architecture.
With separate caches, programs and data can no longer reside in shared main memory.
Von Neumann uses a shared memory for programs and data.
A shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches is one example of a hybrid organization.

questions.explanation: a, b, and c correspond to the three organization types described. Write protection and separate caches do not, by themselves, fully determine the memory organization.

questions.prompt: Because programs reside in main memory in the von Neumann model, the machine can in principle also change program contents.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Programs and data reside in the same memory, and the key points explicitly state that the machine can change memory contents.
concepts: Programs and data in the same memory

questions.prompt: Which technique is given as the usual way to implement different execution paths without changing the program's own code?

options.text: Only clearing main memory
Conditional jumps and changes to addresses
Replacing the ALU with the input/output unit
Storing all instructions as decimal numbers

questions.explanation: Instead of self-modifying code, different execution paths are implemented mainly through conditional jumps and changes to addresses.

questions.prompt: During linking, references are resolved and ___ may be adjusted if necessary.

options.text: address values
input/output units
instruction cycles
register widths

questions.explanation: The linker can adjust address values so that references between the combined program modules point to the correct targets.

questions.prompt: Which statements about optimization and program execution are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The externally observable behavior must be preserved.
Optimization may arbitrarily change the required behavior.
After every optimization, the basic sequential idea applies completely, with no possible jumps.
An optimized program need not have the same instruction sequence as an unoptimized example.
An optimized program need not have the same register allocation as an unoptimized example.

questions.explanation: Optimizations can change register allocation and instruction order. The program's observable behavior must still be preserved, and jumps remain possible.

questions.prompt: A program contains instructions at addresses 200, 201, 202, and 300. The program counter (PC) starts at 200. After each instruction, the PC is incremented by 1 if there is no jump. The instruction at address 201 jumps to address 300 if its condition is met; if the condition is not met, the program continues at the next address. Which sequences give the addresses of the first three instructions executed, once when the condition is met and once when it is not met?
questions.explanation: Execution begins at 200 and proceeds normally to 201. If the condition is not met there, the next address is 202. If it is met, the PC jumps to 300. The two sequences are therefore 200, 201, 202 and 200, 201, 300.

options.text: Data are always ISA instructions; instructions are always decimal data.
Instructions are only in the input/output unit, and data only in registers.
Assembly text is the only possible memory content for instructions.
Data follow an agreed binary interpretation; instructions are encoded according to the ISA and can be represented as assembly language.

questions.prompt: A routine calls a second routine. Which approach correctly preserves the ability to return?

options.text: The return address is not saved because a nested call does not change it.
The stack frame is released before the nested call and is not set up again afterward.
The first return address is saved before the nested call and restored before returning.
All registers must always remain unchanged, regardless of the calling convention.

questions.explanation: A nested `jal` overwrites `ra`. The current return address must therefore be saved and restored before returning.

questions.prompt: When $PC=100$, `jal ra, 20` is executed. What values do `ra` and the new $PC$ have afterward?
questions.explanation: `jal` stores $PC+4=104$ in `ra` and sets $PC$ to $PC+20=120$. The other options confuse the return address with the jump target or calculate the offset incorrectly.

questions.prompt: Which combination correctly describes the stack and main memory?

options.text: The stack is in the input/output unit and is managed word by word without addresses.
The stack is in main memory, which is byte-addressable.
The stack is a memory with its own cells, independent of main memory.
The stack is exclusively in registers and cannot be addressed.

questions.explanation: The stack is an area of byte-addressable main memory. It is not a technically separate memory.

questions.prompt: A program calls `printf` and is linked with a library. Which operations are part of linking? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The reference to `printf` is assigned to a suitable target.
Linking automatically turns von Neumann into a Harvard architecture.
The call to `printf` is fully executed during linking.
The compiled program module and the required library are combined.
Address values are adjusted if necessary.

questions.explanation: Linking combines program modules and libraries, resolves references such as the one to `printf`, and may adjust addresses. It does not execute the call or automatically change the memory architecture.

questions.prompt: A computer has shared main memory for programs and data, separate instruction and data caches, and a program area that cannot be modified. Which classification is correct?

options.text: A pure von Neumann design with no separate memory handling
The hybrid organization described; write protection is independent of it
Harvard architecture, because the program area cannot be modified
Self-modifying code, because programs are in main memory

questions.explanation: Shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches is the hybrid organization described. Write protection concerns how the area is handled and does not, by itself, answer the question of organization.
concepts: Programs and data in the same memory

questions.prompt: A program starts at address $100$. The instruction at $101$ is a conditional jump to $200$, and the condition is true. Which three addresses are executed first?
questions.explanation: Execution begins at $100$ and reaches the jump instruction at $101$. Since the condition is true, the target address $200$ follows instead of the sequential address $102$.

questions.prompt: Adjusting references during linking is the same as self-modifying code.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Linking combines compiled modules and adjusts references or addresses. Self-modifying code, by contrast, changes the program's own code.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly connect the fundamental idea of the von Neumann concept with optimized program execution? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Conditional and unconditional jumps can depart from the sequential order.
A shared main memory automatically means a Harvard architecture.
Optimizations may change internal register allocation and instruction order as long as the observable behavior is preserved.
Self-modifying code is required for every jump.
The computer's structure remains independent of the specific problem; the program controls the computer.

questions.explanation: The general computer concept is controlled by programs, optimizations may change the internal implementation, and jumps can depart from the sequence. Statements b and e contradict the concepts described.

options.text: different
unaddressable
higher only

questions.prompt: In principle, how can the same memory contain both data and instructions?

options.text: Data and instructions must always be stored in separate main memories.
Instructions are interpreted exclusively as decimal data and data exclusively as jumps.
Instructions are not in main memory, but only in the control unit.
Both are encoded memory contents; data are interpreted according to their agreed encoding, and instructions according to the ISA.

questions.explanation: Both data and instructions are stored as encoded contents in shared memory. Their use determines the appropriate interpretation: the agreed data encoding or the ISA encoding.

questions.prompt: On the same smartphone, you open a navigation app, a music app, and Sudoku one after another. What is the architectural idea behind this?

options.text: Prologue and epilogue: Each app thereby has its own processor.
The von Neumann concept: A general-purpose computer is controlled by different programs to perform different tasks.
Harvard architecture: A separate main memory is installed for each app.
Linking: The operating system reconnects the hardware every time an app starts.

questions.explanation: The von Neumann concept separates the computer's structure from the specific problem: the same device can perform very different tasks under the control of different programs.
concepts: Programs and data in the same memory

questions.prompt: You compile a C program in static linking mode that uses `printf`. When the executable is created, the reference to the library function is resolved. Which step is taking place here?

options.text: Epilogue
Conditional jump
Linking
Division into Harvard memories

questions.explanation: During linking, compiled program modules and libraries are combined and references such as the one to `printf` are resolved; in static linking mode, this happens when the executable is created.

questions.prompt: A memory chip labels an area as 1 KiB. How many bytes is that?
questions.explanation: The prefix Ki denotes a power of two: 1 KiB = 2^10 bytes = 1024 bytes.

questions.prompt: When a function is called in an image-editing program, local variables and saved registers are set up. On return, this space is released. What are these two boundary phases called?

questions.prompt: A sensor provides an unsigned measurement value of 12 bits. How many different bit patterns or values are possible?

questions.prompt: You are documenting a truth table for five binary inputs. How many rows does it need to include every input combination?
